title: The 20-Minute Decision Meeting
author: Nick Martin
summary: Martin argues that teams stall on decisions because consensus by default hands every person a veto, and he offers a five-step, 20-minute meeting as a remedy. He illustrates the cost with a team that spent six meetings choosing a project tool that most people favoured from the start. The method names a decider in advance, uses a silent written lean, discusses only the split, and tests the proposal with a live-with-it check before locking in an owner and first step. The move is to replace the standard of agreement with the lower standard of whether a proposal is safe enough to try. He answers the objection that this is just the boss deciding, and he reserves consensus for decisions about team values and norms.
points: Consensus by default lets one holdout delay a decision across many meetings.
Naming the decider before discussion removes the ambiguity that causes the stall.
A silent written lean stops the first or most senior voice from steering the room.
The live-with-it check asks for a lower bar than agreement and invites changes to the proposal.
Consensus is still right for decisions about team values and how people treat each other.
quotes: Nobody wanted to overrule a colleague. So every meeting ended the same way: “Let’s get a bit more input and come back to it.
None of that was anyone’s fault because nobody had said who would make the call. So the group defaulted to everyone. Consensus gives every person in the room a veto.
Everyone writes before anyone speaks. Otherwise the first voice, or the most senior one, sets the direction and the rest adjust to it.
The decider proposes. The room tests the proposal against a lower bar than agreement.
Can you live with it?” is a lower bar than “do you agree?” which is why it works.
In the consensus trap, the decision still gets made. It’s made by whoever holds out longest, or by the deadline.
Decisions about how a team works together, such as its values, its norms and how people treat each other, need everyone on board. Each person has to choose to follow them.
